4.text: we distribute gifts to such spirits on all sides.” Similar contradictory ideas

5.text: may be found, however, among many primitive tribes. Some of them sacri-

6.text: fice chiefly to the evil spirits, arguing that it is of the greatest importance to

7.text: disarm their ill-will. Thus, Urey Lisiansky says of the inhabitants of Kadiak,

8.text: that they believe in the existence of two supernatural beings, one of which is

9.text: good, the other evil. They sacrifice to the latter because they are afraid of

10.text: his ill-will, and say that the former, even without sacrifice, does no harm to

11.text: any one.² Other tribes, on the contrary, intend their sacrifices particularly as

12.text: a means of securing the protection of “spirits” wishing well to the offerer.³

13.text: This is mainly the case with the Chukchee. Perhaps the regularity of the

14.text: sacrifice, from season to season and from year to year, leads primitive man

15.text: to suppose that naturally the recipients of all these offerings will be well

16.text: disposed to the giver, and will provide special protection for the material

17.text: pursuits of his life, since they always receive a share of its fruit.
